claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and phase-homogeneous, with a uniform elemental distribution.
Preferential Cu surface segregation governs the early phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Cu segregation locally lowers the melting point at the nanoparticle surface.
The locally reduced surface melting point triggers formation of a premelting layer.
The premelting layer progressively invades the nanoparticle core.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic mobility causes Cu atoms to migrate toward the nanoparticle surface.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other relevant constituents or the homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu alloy state.
A Cu-enriched surface produces a liquid-like or premelted surface layer.
Surface melting will begin earlier than core melting.
Heating will increase the Cu concentration at the nanoparticle surface relative to the interior.
The surface-melting onset temperature will be lower than that predicted by a homogeneous melting model.
Before heating, the nanoparticles exhibit melting behavior consistent with ideal mixing and lack localized melting initiation.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticle sizes for which surface effects dominate, exemplified as particles below 100 nm.
The proposed mechanism requires heating rates slow enough to permit Cu segregation dynamics.
Surface passivation can reduce the availability of Cu for surface segregation.
The magnitude of the segregation-induced reduction in melting onset may vary with particle size and synthesis conditions.
